title: Telehealth Billing for Behavioral Health in 2026: POS 02 vs 10 and Modifiers 95, 93 and FQ
summary: How to code behavioral health telehealth in 2026: POS 02 vs POS 10, modifiers 95, 93 and FQ, Medicare's extension through 2027 and the 2028 in-person rule, RHC and FQHC billing, three Medicaid examples, DEA prescribing status, and a denial table.
body_markdown:
For Medicare behavioral health telehealth in 2026, report POS 10 when the patient is at home and POS 02 when they're anywhere else, and add modifier 93 when the visit was audio-only (FQ in RHCs and FQHCs). POS 10 pays the non-facility rate and POS 02 the lower facility rate. Many Medicaid programs and commercial plans also want modifier 95 on video visits. As of November 2026, Medicare's telehealth flexibilities run through December 31, 2027.


Telehealth rules changed several times between October 2025 and October 2026, so every statement below carries a date and a source. This guide covers POS and modifier logic, Medicare rules for mental health and substance use disorder (SUD) care at home, RHC and FQHC billing, Medicaid and commercial variation, DEA prescribing status, documentation and two quick-reference tables. For time rules on the codes themselves, see our[psychotherapy CPT code guide](https://blog.adentris.com/psychotherapy-cpt-codes-90832-90834-90837/) .


The short version


- POS 10 means the patient was at home and pays at Medicare's non-facility rate. POS 02 means the patient was somewhere else and pays at the facility rate.
- Modifier 93 marks audio-only. FQ means the same thing on RHC and FQHC claims. Modifier 95 marks audio-video. Many Medicaid and commercial payers require it, while Medicare uses it in a few specific cases.
- The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 extended Medicare's telehealth flexibilities through December 31, 2027. Mental health and SUD telehealth to the home is already permanent.
- Medicare's in-person visit requirement for mental health telehealth now starts January 1, 2028. It doesn't apply to SUD treatment, and patients who start telehealth before 2028 are treated as established.
- DEA's temporary telemedicine prescribing flexibilities expire December 31, 2026. As of November 4, 2026, no fifth extension and no final special registration rule had been published. The buprenorphine telemedicine rule is in effect.


## Before you submit: a six-point telehealth claim checklist


Most telehealth denials in behavioral health come from a mismatch between where the patient was, how the visit happened and what the payer expects. Run these six checks on every claim. The sections below explain each rule.


Check What to confirm Why it matters


**Patient location** Home or another site, recorded in the note Drives POS 10 vs POS 02 and the Medicare payment rate


**Modality** Audio-video or audio-only, and why audio-only was used Audio-only needs modifier 93 (FQ on RHC and FQHC claims)


**Payer rule** Medicare, your state Medicaid program or the commercial plan's current policy Modifier 95 and POS rules differ by payer


**Code eligibility** The code is on the payer's telehealth list A code that isn't allowed by telehealth is denied regardless of documentation


**Note content** Consent, both locations, modality, time and the clinical content Reviewers check telehealth notes against the same standards as in-person notes


**Prescribing** Controlled substances follow current DEA telemedicine rules The temporary DEA flexibilities end December 31, 2026 unless extended again


## Where Medicare telehealth stands as of November 2026


The controlling law is section 6209 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148), signed February 3, 2026. It moved the end date for the pandemic-era flexibilities from January 30, 2026 to December 31, 2027. That covers non-behavioral telehealth from any location, the wider practitioner list, RHCs and FQHCs as distant sites, and audio-only coverage. CMS's Telehealth FAQ, updated October 8, 2026, restates the same dates.


Date What happened What it means for billing


**Oct 1, 2025** Flexibilities lapsed during the federal shutdown CMS later paid these claims as if there had been no lapse


**Nov 2025** Continuing appropriations law (Public Law 119-37) restored them through January 30, 2026 Retroactive to October 1


**Feb 3, 2026** Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 signed Flexibilities through December 31, 2027. In-person rule for mental health moved to January 1, 2028


**Oct 1, 2026** RHCs and FQHCs stop billing G2025 for non-behavioral telehealth (CR 14468) Bill the actual CPT or HCPCS code with 93 or 95


**Nov 4, 2026** CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule released Effective January 1, 2027. Read the rule text before changing January edits


**Jan 1, 2027** New modifiers BB and BC required where they apply, per the CMS FAQ Flags platform contracts and incident-to telehealth. No payment effect


**Jan 1, 2028** Non-behavioral telehealth returns to rural and facility limits. Mental health in-person rule starts Behavioral health telehealth to the home continues


What the dates don't touch matters as much. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 permanently removed geographic and place-of-service limits for behavioral health telehealth, and the home has been a permitted site for SUD treatment since July 2019. So BH programs face no 2028 cliff on location. Will Congress extend the non-behavioral flexibilities again? Nobody knows yet.


## POS 02 vs POS 10: definitions and Medicare payment


Both codes describe the patient's location, not the clinician's. CMS defines them this way in its MLN telehealth booklet:


- **POS 02, Telehealth Provided Other than in Patient's Home:** the patient isn't at home. Think a clinic exam room, a school, a workplace, or a residential treatment facility.
- **POS 10, Telehealth Provided in Patient's Home:** the patient is in a private residence, which CMS describes as a location other than a hospital or other facility where the patient receives care.


Since January 1, 2024, Medicare pays POS 10 claims at the non-facility PFS rate and POS 02 claims at the facility rate. For most psychotherapy codes the facility rate is lower, because it assumes a facility carries part of the practice expense. Picking POS 02 out of habit for a patient at home leaves money on the table. Picking POS 10 for a patient sitting in your residential unit overstates payment and invites a recoupment.


Two edge cases come up in BH. If the clinician works inside a hospital and the patient is at home, CMS's CY 2024 rule says to bill the hospital POS with modifier 95. And a clinician working from home doesn't change the POS. CMS lets them bill from their physical practice location, and only virtual-only practitioners must enroll a home address.


## Telehealth modifiers in 2026: 95, 93, FQ, FR, GT, BB and BC


Modifier Meaning Medicare use in 2026 Medicaid and commercial


**95** Synchronous audio-video Hospital-based clinician with patient at home (hospital POS), hospital-employed PT, OT or SLP, RHC and FQHC video visits, OTP services by video The usual video marker. Texas Medicaid requires it. NY OASAS accepts 95 or GT


**93** Synchronous audio-only Required on every audio-only telehealth claim under 42 CFR 410.78(a)(3) Texas uses it for non-behavioral audio-only. NY OASAS accepts 93 or FQ


**FQ** Service furnished using audio-only technology RHCs and FQHCs may use FQ, 93 or both. CMS calls them identical in meaning Texas Medicaid requires FQ for behavioral health audio-only


**FR** Supervising practitioner present by two-way audio-video Appended when the supervisor was present virtually, not in the room Varies by payer


**GT** Interactive audio and video (legacy) Only on institutional claims from CAH Method II providers Some state programs still use it


**BB, BC** Virtual platform arrangement, and telehealth furnished incident to Required starting January 1, 2027, per the CMS Telehealth FAQ Not applicable


Modifier 95 is where most confusion sits. In its CY 2024 rule, CMS said 95 applies when the clinician is in the hospital and the patient is at home, and to outpatient therapy furnished by hospital PT, OT and SLP staff. For ordinary professional claims, POS 02 or 10 already tells Medicare the visit was telehealth. If your templates still append 95 to Medicare claims, check your MAC's current edit before you strip it.


BB and BC come from section 6209(g) of the 2026 law, which told CMS to flag telehealth delivered through a contracted or paid virtual platform and telehealth billed incident to. CMS says they carry no payment implications. If you use a telehealth platform or bill staff incident to a supervisor, plan the claim change now.


FR rarely matters in outpatient BH, because 42 CFR 410.26 lets auxiliary personnel furnish behavioral health services incident to under general supervision.


## Medicare rules for mental health and SUD telehealth


### The in-person visit requirement


As of November 2026, it isn't in effect. Section 1834(m)(7)(B) of the Social Security Act, as amended in February 2026, applies it to mental health telehealth furnished on or after January 1, 2028. From then, a clinician needs an in-person, non-telehealth service within 6 months before the first mental health telehealth visit and, per CMS regulation, at least once every 12 months after.


Three details soften it. Per CMS's FAQ, patients who begin mental health telehealth at home before 2028 skip the 6-month test and only need the annual visit. Under 42 CFR 410.78(b)(3)(xiv), clinician and patient can agree an in-person visit's risks outweigh its benefits for a year, if the reason is documented. And a same-specialty colleague in the group can do the visit.


The requirement doesn't apply at all to telehealth for a diagnosed SUD or a co-occurring mental health disorder. The statute says so in section 1834(m)(7)(B)(ii). Make sure the SUD diagnosis is documented and on the claim, since it's the basis for the exemption.


### Audio-only


Through December 31, 2027, beneficiaries can receive audio-only telehealth at home under the statute. After that, CMS's permanent rule still allows audio-only behavioral health at home when the clinician is technically capable of video and the patient isn't capable of, or doesn't consent to, video. Either way, append 93 (or FQ in an RHC or FQHC). The modifier is your attestation that those conditions were met, so the note should say why video wasn't used.


### Codes and practitioners


Psychotherapy and the psychiatric diagnostic evaluations are on the Medicare telehealth list, and CMS added 90849 for 2026. Our[90791 vs 90792 guide](https://blog.adentris.com/cpt-90791-vs-90792-psychiatric-diagnostic-evaluation/) covers who may bill each evaluation, and the[behavioral health CPT guide](https://blog.adentris.com/cpt-codes-behavioral-health-guide/) covers the rest. Marriage and family therapists and mental health counselors are eligible distant site practitioners.


One trap: in the CY 2025 rule, CMS declined to pay the telemedicine E/M codes 98000 to 98015. Psychiatric E/M visits go on 99202 to 99215 with the right POS.


## RHC and FQHC billing for mental health telehealth


Since 2022, an RHC or FQHC mental health visit can be furnished by audio-video, or by audio-only when the patient can't use or declines video. It's paid under the all-inclusive rate or FQHC PPS like any visit. The Benefit Policy Manual, Chapter 13, section 170 (revised February 2026) says to append 95 for video and 93 for audio-only. FQ works in place of 93.


The in-person requirement for these virtual mental health visits also moved to January 1, 2028 under section 6209(d). Group mental health services still don't qualify as an RHC or FQHC visit, because they aren't a one-on-one encounter.


Non-behavioral telehealth changed on October 1, 2026. Under CR 14468, RHCs and FQHCs no longer report the single code G2025. They bill the individual CPT or HCPCS code for the distant site service, with the revenue code and modifier 93 or 95. Payment stays at a PFS-average rate through December 31, 2027.


## Medicaid: three states, three different answers


Medicaid sets its own telehealth rules state by state, and BH carve-outs add another layer. Per the Center for Connected Health Policy's Fall 2025 survey, 46 states and DC pay for audio-only telephone services in some capacity, often with limits. The modifiers and POS rules differ more than the coverage does.


Program Audio-video Audio-only POS Other rule worth knowing


**Texas Medicaid** (TMPPM, November 2026) 95 FQ for behavioral health, 93 for other services Not addressed in this handbook Informed consent before an audio-only BH service. Verbal consent is fine if it's documented


**New York OASAS** (APG manual, October 2026) 95 on Appendix P codes, GT where 95 can't be used FQ or 93 Not needed for OASAS claims Same rate codes and procedure codes as in-person


**California Drug Medi-Cal State Plan** (billing manual v4.0, July 2026) Not specified in the manual Not specified in the manual 02 or 10 for any telehealth or telephone service Outpatient lines without a POS are denied


The lesson: a Medicare-built claim edit will misfire on Medicaid. A Texas audio-only therapy claim with 93 instead of FQ, or a Drug Medi-Cal phone session sent with POS 11, fails for reasons Medicare would never flag. Build edits payer by payer, including each MCO's telehealth policy.


## Commercial plans and telehealth parity laws


State law reaches fully insured commercial plans. Per CCHP's Fall 2025 summary, 44 states, DC, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands have a private payer law that addresses telehealth reimbursement. Not all of them require payment parity. Only 24 states and Puerto Rico explicitly require telehealth to be paid at the same rate as in-person care.


Self-funded ERISA plans generally sit outside state insurance mandates, so a parity statute may not cover much of your commercial volume. Check each plan's covered modalities, accepted POS codes, modifier rules, audio-only code list and contract rates.


## DEA telemedicine prescribing for controlled substances, as of November 2026


The Ryan Haight Act generally requires an in-person medical evaluation before a practitioner prescribes a controlled substance remotely. The fourth temporary DEA and HHS extension, published December 31, 2025, waives that through December 31, 2026. It allows Schedule II to V prescribing by audio-video telemedicine without a prior in-person visit, and Schedule III to V opioid use disorder medications by audio-only.


A permanent pathway already exists for buprenorphine. Under 21 CFR 1306.51, in effect since December 31, 2025, a prescriber may treat OUD by audio-only or audio-video after reviewing the state PDMP and recording the date and time. Prescribing under it is capped at six calendar months, then needs an in-person evaluation or another lawful route.


Here's what's genuinely unclear. As of early November 2026, the Federal Register shows neither DEA's final special registration rule nor a fifth extension of the telemedicine flexibilities. If nothing changes by January 1, 2027, prescribing a stimulant or benzodiazepine by telemedicine would generally require a prior in-person evaluation. Find patients on those medications who've never been seen in person, and offer visits before year end.


OTPs follow 42 CFR 8.12, which allows the admission examination by telehealth. For methadone that means audio-video. Audio-only is allowed only when video isn't available and the patient is with a practitioner registered to prescribe controlled medications.


## Documentation every telehealth note needs


Payers audit telehealth claims against the note. Per CCHP, 45 states, DC and Puerto Rico have some telehealth consent requirement. Build these fields into the template so nobody has to remember them:


- **Consent.** Written or verbal, as your state requires, with who gave it and when.
- **Patient location.** Where the patient physically was, including the state. It drives POS, licensure and some Medicaid rules.
- **Provider location.** At least city and state.
- **Modality and why.** Audio-video or audio-only. For audio-only, record that the patient couldn't use or declined video. If video dropped mid-session, say when.
- **Time.** Start and stop times, or total time, for time-based codes such as 90832 to 90837.
- **Participants.** Anyone else present, including interpreters.
- **In-person tracking.** Date of the last in-person visit for Medicare mental health patients, and the documented reason if you skip the annual visit after 2027.
- **PDMP review.** Date and time, for any buprenorphine prescription under 21 CFR 1306.51.


## Quick decision table: which POS and modifier


Scenario Medicare professional claim Medicare RHC or FQHC Medicaid Commercial


**Video, patient at home** POS 10 Revenue code with 95 State rule. Texas: 95. CA Drug Medi-Cal: POS 02 or 10 Plan policy. Confirm POS and whether 95 is required


**Video, patient at a clinic or facility** POS 02 Revenue code with 95 State rule. Texas: 95. CA Drug Medi-Cal: POS 02 Plan policy. Confirm POS and whether 95 is required


**Audio-only, patient at home** POS 10 with 93 93 or FQ Texas: FQ for BH. NY OASAS: FQ or 93 Confirm audio-only coverage first, then the modifier


**Audio-only, patient not at home** Generally not payable. CMS limits audio-only to patients at home 93 or FQ. RHC and FQHC originating sites aren't limited to the home State rule Plan policy


**Clinician in hospital, patient at home, video** Hospital POS with 95 Not applicable State rule Plan policy


## Common telehealth errors and the denials they cause


Error Codes you may see on the 835 Fix


POS 10 billed for a patient who was in a facility, or the reverse CO-58 or CO-5 Set POS from the documented patient location, then send a corrected claim


Audio-only visit billed without 93 or FQ, or billed with 95 CO-4, often with N822 or N823 Match the modifier to the modality in the note


Missing or invalid POS CO-16 with M77 Add a valid POS and resubmit


Service not on the payer's telehealth list billed with POS 02 or 10 CO-96 with N776 (Medicare) Check the list before scheduling the visit as telehealth


Clinician not licensed in the patient's state, or not an eligible telehealth practitioner CO-185 Verify licensure and enrollment against the patient's location


Read the remark code before you rework anything. ## Frequently asked questions


**What is the difference between POS 02 and POS 10?**


Both mark a telehealth visit, and both describe where the patient was. POS 10 means the patient was at home. POS 02 means the patient was somewhere other than home, such as a clinic or facility. Since January 1, 2024, Medicare pays POS 10 at the non-facility rate and POS 02 at the facility rate.


**Is modifier 95 required on Medicare telehealth claims in 2026?**


Not on most professional claims. CMS's CY 2024 rule ties modifier 95 to a clinician in the hospital treating a patient at home, billed with the hospital POS, and to hospital-employed therapists. RHCs and FQHCs use 95 for video visits, and many Medicaid and commercial payers want it. Check your MAC's current edits before removing it.


**When do I use modifier 93 and when do I use FQ?**


Both mean the visit was audio-only. Medicare requires 93 on audio-only telehealth claims, and RHCs and FQHCs may use FQ, 93 or both because CMS treats them as identical. Medicaid programs differ. Texas Medicaid, for example, requires FQ for behavioral health audio-only services and 93 for other audio-only services.


**Are Medicare telehealth flexibilities extended past 2026?**


Yes. As of November 2026, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 extends them through December 31, 2027. Behavioral health telehealth to the patient's home is permanent and doesn't depend on that date. Whether the non-behavioral flexibilities will be extended beyond 2027 is not yet known.


**Does Medicare require an in-person visit for mental health telehealth?**


Not until January 1, 2028. From then, new mental health telehealth patients need an in-person visit within 6 months before the first telehealth visit, then generally one every 12 months. Patients who start before 2028 only need the annual visit, and the rule doesn't apply to SUD treatment or a co-occurring mental health disorder.


**Can buprenorphine still be prescribed by telehealth after 2026?**


Yes, under 21 CFR 1306.51, which took effect December 31, 2025. A practitioner can prescribe buprenorphine for opioid use disorder through audio-only or audio-video after checking the state PDMP, for up to six calendar months. Continuing after that requires an in-person evaluation or another pathway the law allows.
